# How to Summarize a Long Email Thread in Apple Mail with Apple Intelligence

> **In short:** In Apple Mail, Apple Intelligence can summarize a long email thread so you can decide quickly whether to read it all. Summaries need a compatible Apple device with Apple Intelligence turned on. Always check the summary against the messages before you act on it.

You're about to start your workday and find a reply-all chain with forty messages, three people arguing about a date, and a question buried somewhere in the middle. By the end of this guide, you'll know how to pull a short summary out of a thread like that, sharpen it into two clear sentences, and check it before you rely on it. This is written for anyone who lives in a busy inbox, especially at work.

## Before you start

- **A compatible Apple device** (a recent iPhone, iPad, or Mac) with **Apple Intelligence** turned on. Apple publishes a list of supported devices and languages, so check that list if you're unsure. Summaries may not be available in every language or region.
- **The Apple Mail app**, and a thread of at least 10 messages so you can see the difference a summary makes.
- **Time needed:** about 10 minutes the first time, then a minute or two per thread.

I'm assuming you already know how to open Mail and read a message. Apple Intelligence is included with supported devices, but if a screen ever asks you to pay for it, stop and check Apple's official website first.

## Step 1 — Confirm Apple Intelligence is turned on

Open the **Settings** app on your iPhone or iPad, or **System Settings** on your Mac. Look for an entry named **Apple Intelligence & Siri**, or a similar label with "Intelligence" in it. Open it and check that the switch for Apple Intelligence is on. You may need to finish a short setup screen first.

Apple Intelligence works in the background, so you won't see a big button for it on this screen. Once it's on, it shows up inside apps like Mail. If you can't find this section, search Settings for "Apple Intelligence," since menus shift between software versions.

💬 Example: No typing is needed in this step.

You'll know it worked when the Apple Intelligence switch is on and nothing on the screen says it's unavailable for your device or language.

## Step 2 — Open the long thread and look for a summary

Open Mail and tap or click the long thread you want to understand. Don't read it yet. Look at the top of the thread, above the first message. In many versions of Mail, a short summary appears there as a few lines of text, sometimes with a label like "Summary" and a small arrow or expand button.

If you don't see one, look for a button or menu item that says **Summarize**, or an icon of sparkles or a pen with lines, which often signals Apple Intelligence features. Tap it, or open the menu next to the thread and choose the summary option. If nothing appears, the thread may be too short, the message may not support summaries, or the feature may not be available on your device yet. Try a different long thread to check.

💬 Example: No typing is needed here either. Just scroll to the top of the thread.

You'll know it worked when a short paragraph appears above the messages, describing who is involved and what the thread is mostly about.

## Step 3 — Ask for a summary that focuses on what you need

Sometimes the default summary is too general. Here's a more useful technique: tell the assistant what you care about. If you have Writing Tools available (look for a pencil-and-lines icon or a **Writing Tools** option when you select text), select the thread's summary text, or select a message you want to condense, and choose a summary option. Some versions also let you type your own request.

When you can type a request, be specific. Name the decision you're looking for, the people who matter, and the timeframe. This keeps the summary focused instead of rambling through every "thanks!" reply. Remember that email is private: only paste or select content you're allowed to share with an AI feature, and follow your workplace's rules.

💬 Example: "Summarize this email thread in three bullet points. Focus on any decisions made and any deadlines for [your team name]."

You'll know it worked when the new summary mentions the decisions and deadlines you asked about, and leaves out most of the small talk.

## Step 4 — Compress the summary into exactly two sentences

Now you can build on the earlier answer. Copy the three-bullet summary from Step 3 (select it, then use the copy option, or press Command-C on a Mac or long-press to copy on a phone). Then ask for the two-sentence version. Giving it a clear word limit helps the assistant stop when you need it to.

Your first sentence should say what the thread is about. Your second should say what, if anything, you need to do. If the answer runs longer than two sentences, ask it again and add "Keep it to exactly two sentences." If the answer is too vague, add a detail, such as the project name or the person who asked the question.

💬 Example: "Using the bullets above, write exactly two sentences. The first says what this thread is about, and the second says what action, if any, [your name] needs to take."

You'll know it worked when you have two sentences you could read aloud to a coworker and they'd understand the situation in a few seconds.

## Step 5 — Check the summary against the messages

This step matters most. AI summaries can miss a detail, mix up who said what, or sound confident about something that was only suggested. Before you forward the summary or make a decision, check the key facts. Find the message the summary mentions (search for a name, a date, or a number), and read that one message yourself. Scroll through the thread's first and last few messages too, because those often hold the start and the conclusion.

If a fact in the summary doesn't match the email, trust the email. You can also ask the assistant to show which message a point came from, though it may not always answer correctly, so verify it yourself.

💬 Example: "Which message did you base the deadline on? Quote the sender's name and the date if you can."

You'll know it worked when every fact in your two-sentence summary matches a message you've actually read.

## Step 6 — Decide whether you need to read the whole thread

Now you can make the decision the summary was meant to support. If the two sentences tell you that nothing is required from you, you can archive the thread or mark it as read. If they say you need to respond, reply to the one message that asks for it. If the thread involves a contract, a policy, a payment, or anything with legal or financial weight, read the full thread and talk to the right person, because a summary is a shortcut, not a substitute for judgment.

It's also worth knowing what summaries can't do. They can't read the attachments inside the thread for you, they can't know your team's history, and they can't tell you what your boss expects. They also can't decide what's important to you.

💬 Example: No typing is needed for this step, but you can jot down your decision in a note.

You'll know it worked when you can state, in one sentence, whether you need to take action on this thread and why.

## Common mistakes

- **Trusting the summary without checking.** The fix: verify any name, date, or number against the original message before you act on it.
- **Pasting sensitive content into an AI feature without thinking.** The fix: only summarize what your workplace allows, and ask your manager or IT team when you're unsure.
- **Expecting a summary on every thread.** The fix: if no summary appears, try a longer thread, check that Apple Intelligence is on, and confirm your device is supported.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** Long group chats and family email threads about travel or events can be summarized in seconds, so you can find the plan without rereading everything.
- **For your business or work:** Use a two-sentence summary to triage your inbox each morning, then give the threads that need action your full attention.
- **If you want to go further:** Try asking the assistant to turn a thread's decisions into a short checklist you can paste into your task app, then review it yourself before you use it.

## Try it now

Open your longest email thread in Mail, look for a summary above the messages, and if one appears, compare it with the first and last messages. If nothing appears, check Settings for Apple Intelligence and try a different thread. You'll be able to see in under two minutes whether a summary saves you time.
